title: Ocular Tuberculosis: The Great Masquerader
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to the diagnosis, classification, and management of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infections affecting the visual system. This resource integrates the latest COTS (Collaborative Ocular Tuberculosis Study) guidelines with gold-standard anatomical and pharmacological protocols.

sections.title: 1. Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Ocular Tuberculosis is an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tb) that can affect any part of the eye, its adnexa, or the optic nerve. It is often a manifestation of extra-pulmonary TB (EPTB) and can occur in the absence of active systemic or pulmonary disease. It presents either through direct tissue invasion by the bacilli or as a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction (Type IV) to mycobacterial antigens.

sections.title: 4. Pathophysiology Mechanisms
content: 1. Inhalation of droplet nuclei containing M. tuberculosis.
2. Primary pulmonary infection and Ghon complex formation.
3. Hematogenous dissemination via alveolar capillaries to the uveal tract (highly vascular).
4. Latency within the RPE or uveal macrophages.
5. Reactivation: Direct bacterial multiplication vs. Immune-mediated inflammation (Delayed Hypersensitivity).

sections.title: 5. Ocular Examination Findings
content: Anterior: 'Mutton-fat' Keratic Precipitates (KPs), Koeppe/Busacca nodules.
Sclera: Necrotizing or non-necrotizing anterior scleritis.
Choroid: Unifocal/Multifocal tubercles (yellowish-white lesions).
Retina: Perivasculitis (predominantly venulitis) and Eales Disease.
Vitreous: 'Snowball' opacities or dense vitritis in endophthalmitis cases.

rows: Yellow-gray nodules (0.5 - 3mm) usually at the posterior pole.
Multifocal, amoeboid, non-contiguous lesions. Start in periphery.
Unlike classic Serpiginous, SLC often spares the peripapillary area initially.
Large solitary subretinal mass (up to 10mm) with exudative detachment.
Peripheral retinal perivasculitis, non-perfusion, and neovascularization.
Primarily affects young healthy males in India/Middle East.

sections.title: 7. Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Detailed History (Systemic symptoms, exposure, travel).
Step 2: TST (Mantoux) >10mm (endemic) or >5mm (high risk/HIV).
Step 3: IGRA (QuantiFERON-TB Gold) for higher specificity.
Step 4: Imaging: Chest X-ray and HRCT Chest (Hilar lymphadenopathy).
Step 5: Ocular Fluids: PCR for IS6110 sequence or mpb64.
Step 6: Gold Standard (Rarely possible): Culture on Lowenstein-Jensen medium.

rows: Bilateral, serous detachments, diffuse uveal thickening, sunset-glow fundus.
Focal retinochoroiditis adjacent to a pigmented scar.

sections.title: 9. COTS Diagnostic Criteria
content: Definite Ocular TB: M. tb found in ocular fluids/tissues via culture or PCR.
Probable Ocular TB: Ocular signs + positive TST/IGRA + systemic TB evidence (Chest HRCT).
Possible Ocular TB: Ocular signs + positive TST/IGRA, but no systemic evidence on imaging.

rows: Monthly Visual Acuity, Color Vision (Ishihara), Humphrey Visual Field (HVF 10-2)

sections.title: 11. Treatment Regimen & Duration
content: Intensive Phase (2 Months): HRPE (Four drugs daily).
Continuation Phase (4-7 Months): HR (Two drugs daily).
Note: Total duration usually 6-9 months; extended to 12 months in CNS involvement or slow responders.

sections.title: 12. Corticosteroid Adjunct Protocol
content: Mandatory to control 'Paradoxical Reaction' (worsening after starting ATT).
Oral Prednisolone: 1 mg/kg/day started 48-72 hours after initiating ATT.
Slow Taper: Reduce over 6-12 weeks depending on clinical response.
Topical: Prednisolone Acetate 1% for anterior segment inflammation.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags & Critical Warnings
content: Ethambutol Toxicity: Progressive, painless bilateral vision loss and red-green color deficiency. Discontinue drug immediately if suspected.
Paradoxical Reaction (Jarisch-Herxheimer-like): Rapid worsening of uveitis/vitritis shortly after ATT initiation. Increase steroid dose.
Multidrug-Resistant (MDR-TB): Failure to respond to ATT after 2 months of compliant therapy.
Adrenal Crisis: If steroids are tapered too rapidly after long-term use.

content.explanation: Standard ATT: Rifampin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol.
Choroidal tubercles, Creeping (Serpiginous), Conglomerate (Tuberculoma), Caseous (Necrosis), Chronic, Contiguous.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: COTS-1 Study: Confirmed that starting ATT in confirmed/probable TB reduces recurrence of uveitis by >50%.
Ultra-sensitive PCR: Targetting repetitive elements like IS6110 improves diagnostic yield in aqueous samples.
Interferon-Gamma Release Assays (IGRA): Now preferred over Mantoux in BCG-vaccinated populations due to higher specificity.

sections.title: 17. Complications & Prognosis
content: Complicated Cataract (due to chronic inflammation or steroids).
Secondary Glaucoma (Trabeculitis or Pupillary Block).
Tractional Retinal Detachment (Eales Disease).
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) - most common cause of vision loss.
Optic Atrophy (Ethambutol or chronic papillitis).

sections.title: 18. High-Yield Clinical Pearls
content: TB can mimic any intraocular inflammation; always test for TB in granulomatous or refractory uveitis.
Negative Chest X-ray does NOT rule out Ocular TB; perform HRCT Chest if suspicion is high.
Eales Disease is a diagnosis of exclusion: think TB first in a young man with peripheral retinal perivasculitis.
Always check baseline visual fields and color vision BEFORE starting Ethambutol.
ATT without steroids in Ocular TB may lead to severe inflammatory damage due to the release of mycobacterial antigens.
